headline: Thompson's group F, a famous group of interval stretchings, is not amenable.
scope: The result is about Thompson's group F only, the dyadic piecewise-linear moves of the interval from 0 to 1.
plain: Thompson's group F is made of ways to stretch and squeeze the interval from 0 to 1. A group is amenable if it admits a fair average that its moves do not change. This paper proves that F has no such average. It finds a fixed finite list of moves that always shifts a positive share of any finite set. This settles a conjecture Geoghegan made in 1979.
doesNot: This does not give an explicit size for the shifted share in its Lean statement. Its two consequences rest on companion papers.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Geoghegan, conjecture that F is nonamenable
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles a 47-year-old conjecture about a central example in group theory. Earlier claims went both ways.

explanation:
Here is one move in Thompson's group F. Take the interval from 0 to 1 and cut it into three pieces. The first half shrinks to half its length. The next quarter slides left by 1/4. The last quarter doubles in length. So 1/2 lands on 1/4, 3/4 lands on 1/2, and 1 stays at 1. Call this move A.

Every cut point of A is a dyadic fraction, meaning a fraction whose bottom number is a power of 2. Every stretch factor is a power of 2, such as 1/2, 1 or 2. Thompson's group F is the collection of all such moves with finitely many pieces. It is a group: doing one move after another gives another move, and every move can be undone. Order matters. Let B leave the left half alone and do a half-size copy of A on the right half. Then A after B sends 3/4 to 3/8. B after A sends 3/4 to 1/2.

Now a question about balance, first in a simpler group. Take the whole numbers and one move: add 1. The set 1 to 100, shifted by 1, becomes 2 to 101. Only two numbers differ between the old set and the new one: 1 and 101. That is 2 out of 100, or 2 percent. For the set 1 to 1000 it drops to 0.2 percent. So the whole numbers have finite sets that barely notice the move.

A group is called amenable if it has a fair way to average every bounded function on it. Fair means the average does not change when you shift the function by any move. This idea goes back to von Neumann and Day. A criterion of Følner from 1955 links it to the example above. Suppose a group is amenable. Then any finite list of moves has finite sets that each move barely shifts. The share that changes can be made as small as you like.

This paper proves that Thompson's group F is not amenable. It fixes one finite list of moves in F. Then it shows that every nonempty finite set of moves has a weak spot. At least one move on the list shifts a fixed positive share of it. No set can push that share toward zero, the way 2 percent fell to 0.2 percent. By Følner's criterion, F cannot be amenable.

The question is old. Thompson introduced F in 1965. Geoghegan conjectured in 1979 that F is not amenable. The usual test does not help. A group that contains a free subgroup cannot be amenable. A free subgroup is a pair of moves that obey no shortcut rules when combined. Brin and Squier showed in 1985 that F contains no free subgroup. Yet F also lies outside the simplest family of amenable groups, called elementary amenable. Neither fact decides the question.

Finite sets were the main way in, and they proved slippery. Moore showed that any barely shifted sets in F would have to be enormous, growing like a tower of powers. Complete answers were claimed in both directions. Shavgulidze claimed amenability, and Moore identified errors in that approach. Moore withdrew his own amenability claim after Akhmedov identified an error in it. Akhmedov's 2021 version claims nonamenability by a different method.

The paper plays two facts against each other. The first is a 1983 result of Benyamini and Sternfeld about infinite-dimensional spaces. There, a ball has a map into itself that moves every point by at least a fixed distance. The map also never stretches distances by more than a fixed factor. The paper gives each dyadic cutting of the interval a color, which is a point in that ball. The color comes from applying the map to the average color of smaller pieces. If F had barely shifted sets, averaging colors over one would give a point the map almost leaves in place. That contradicts the fixed minimum distance. The list of moves is chosen before the set, so no set can dodge it.

The result says what F is not. It does not describe F in any new positive way. The Lean statement gives no explicit size for the shifted share and names no particular generating moves. The paper also draws two consequences, about special representations of F and about random networks built on it. Those rely on separate companion papers, not on this proof.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal statement. It rules out a fair average on F, the standard group of dyadic piecewise-linear moves of the interval. A Comparator statement for it is listed. The Lean scope note covers nonamenability only, not the two consequences. No specialists have published a review yet.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. A Lean formalization of nonamenability is listed with a Comparator statement. The two consequences are not in the Lean scope note, and no specialist review has been published.

glossary.meaning: All increasing piecewise-linear stretchings of the interval from 0 to 1 with finitely many pieces, dyadic cut points and slopes that are powers of 2.
A fraction whose bottom number is a power of 2, such as 3/8.
A collection of moves where doing two in a row gives another, and every move can be undone.
A group with a fair way to average bounded functions on it that its own moves do not change.
Moves inside a group that obey no shortcut rules when combined; having one rules out amenability.
The simplest family of amenable groups, built from finite and abelian groups by standard steps.
A computer program that checks each step of a mathematical proof written in its formal language.
